questions.title: Is MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent mandatory before any adenoma is managed as an adenoma, and who may waive it?
questions.question: Is MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent mandatory before any adenoma is managed as an adenoma, and who may waive it?

positions.says: MRI is superior to all other modalities and can subtype up to 80% of adenomas (II-2, grade 1); contrast ultrasound separates adenoma from FNH but cannot subtype.
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Standard 'Make the diagnosis on contrast-enhanced MRI…' (preferred-for and note)

positions.says: Adds that a hepatobiliary agent has particular value for identifying focal nodular hyperplasia.
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Standard 'Make the diagnosis on contrast-enhanced MRI…'

positions.says: Prospective multicentre cohort: 18 of 66 women (27%) referred with a suspected sub-5 cm adenoma had FNH on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI; the authors held that this misdiagnosis rate justifies the scan, if only to prevent unnecessary anxiety.
positions.locator: Gate 6 · Standard 'Confirm the diagnosis on MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent…'

positions.says: Of 222 Dutch resections for presumed adenoma, 43% had a changed final diagnosis; absence of hepatobiliary MRI independently predicted change (aOR 1.8), an effect the roadmap says is confounded by era and centre.
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Standard 'Make the diagnosis on contrast-enhanced MRI…' (caveat and note)

questions.divergence: Sources agree that hepatobiliary-contrast MRI sharpens the adenoma-versus-FNH distinction, but none makes it mandatory or addresses who may waive it, access or cost, and the audit's effect size is confounded.
questions.proposal: Contrast-enhanced MRI for every patient, with a hepatobiliary agent whenever the question is adenoma versus FNH and always before pregnancy counselling; board triage returns an uncharacterised lesion for imaging rather than discussing it. The roadmap names no one who may waive the requirement.
questions.proposal_locator: Gate 1 · Standard 'Make the diagnosis on contrast-enhanced MRI…'; Gate 6 · Standard 'Confirm the diagnosis on MRI with a hepatobiliary contrast agent…'; The board meeting · Triage
questions.rationale: 27% of referred sub-5 cm lesions proved to be focal nodular hyperplasia on hepatobiliary-contrast MRI in the prospective cohort — a lesion needing no follow-up at all. This is an access and cost question as much as a clinical one, so it needs a written answer rather than a preference.
questions.audit: Audit: proportion characterised before first board discussion, and proportion whose diagnosis changed.

questions.title: Does the programme adopt routine subtyping — a standing four-antibody panel on every specimen and biopsy, with CTNNB1 exon and codon sequencing where activation is suspected, and prostaglandin D synthase for the sonic hedgehog subgroup?
questions.question: Does the programme adopt routine subtyping — a standing four-antibody panel on every specimen and biopsy, with CTNNB1 exon and codon sequencing where activation is suspected, and prostaglandin D synthase for the sonic hedgehog subgroup?

positions.says: No justification for recommending histopathology or molecular subtyping as routine practice; biopsy may be considered within a benign-tumour MDT to exclude malignancy; imaging-based subtyping needs prospective validation first.
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Reasonable 'Biopsy when the imaging is atypical…' (caveat); Gate 2 · Reasonable 'Where the subtype is known and low risk…' (caveat)

positions.locator: Gate 1 · Reasonable 'Biopsy when the imaging is atypical…'

positions.says: Reserves biopsy for cases where imaging is inconclusive (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence).
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Reasonable 'Biopsy when the imaging is atypical…'

positions.says: Only 27% of 33 beta-catenin-mutated adenomas showed the strong homogeneous glutamine synthetase pattern and S45 lesions are hard to recognise; the authors call for revised immunohistochemical criteria or mutation screening.
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Reasonable 'Where tissue exists, ask for the four-antibody panel…' (caveat)

positions.locator: Gate 1 · Standard subtype option 'Sonic hedgehog (shHCA)'; Gate 1 · Reasonable 'Where tissue exists, ask for the four-antibody panel…' (pref); What we are not sure about #9

questions.divergence: EASL rejects routine subtyping while the Italian guideline, the molecular literature and the local transplant protocol's molecular route presuppose it, and the two subtypes that matter most can be identified reliably only by sequencing.
questions.proposal: Biopsy is reserved for atypical imaging, suspected transformation or a subtype that would change management. On tissue that exists, the board model makes the four-antibody panel standard and requests CTNNB1 exon and codon where activation is suspected, a transplant route may apply, or the patient is male. Whether to subtype routinely is left to the group.

questions.title: How long may risk-factor modification run before a persistent lesion over 5 cm is treated — EASL's 6 months, or 12, or longer in a lesion that is still falling?
questions.question: How long may risk-factor modification run before a persistent lesion over 5 cm is treated — EASL's 6 months, or 12, or longer in a lesion that is still falling?

positions.says: Reassess every presumed adenoma with contrast MRI at 6 months; in women, resection is indicated for a nodule still 5 cm or more (II-3, grade 2). EASL also says no robust data define the timeline of stable disease.
positions.locator: Gate 2 · Standard 'Reimage with contrast-enhanced MRI at 6 months…'; Gate 2 · Reasonable 'Extend observation past 12 months…' (note)

positions.says: Uses a looser 6- to 12-month imaging interval not tied to a size trigger (conditional, low quality), and holds that lesions of 5 cm or more warrant intervention.
positions.locator: Gate 2 · Standard 'Reimage with contrast-enhanced MRI at 6 months…'; Gate 4 · Standard 'Treat a lesion that is persistently larger than 5 cm…'

positions.says: MRI 6 months after stopping contraception, repeated at 1 year if unchanged or reduced below 5 cm, then annual ultrasound after the first 18 months; every step, including the 6-month decision point, is graded very low quality (D), conditional.
positions.locator: Gate 2 · Standard 'Reimage with contrast-enhanced MRI at 6 months…'; Gate 4 · Standard (caveat)

positions.says: Of 194 patients with adenomas over 5 cm, 8.5-15.3% had regressed below 5 cm at 26 weeks against 58.5% eventually (median 104 weeks), without complications. The authors propose 12 months for typical non-beta-catenin adenomas in women. 47 of 241 were excluded for short follow-up.
positions.locator: Gate 2 · Standard 'Reimage with contrast-enhanced MRI at 6 months…' (caveat and note); Gate 2 · Reasonable 'Extend observation past 12 months…'

positions.says: 48 of 61 responding experts (79%) advise against routine resection above 5 cm after lifestyle change; the roadmap notes a 21% response rate and stated rather than observed practice.
positions.locator: Gate 2 · Avoid 'Do not operate on a large adenoma at 6 months…'

questions.divergence: EASL anchors the decision at 6 months, while ACG uses a looser 6- to 12-month interval. The regression cohort, its authors and most surveyed experts favour waiting longer. The authors' 12-month proposal ignores baseline diameter even though time to regression was strongly size-dependent.
questions.proposal: Reimage with contrast MRI at 6 months and read it as a trajectory; do not call risk-factor modification a failure before 12 months (grade C, a deliberate deviation from EASL). Observation beyond 12 months is Reasonable in a woman with a typical, non-beta-catenin adenoma that is shrinking. No diameter-specific interval is proposed.
questions.proposal_locator: What we are not sure about #4; Gate 2 · Standard 'Reimage with contrast-enhanced MRI at 6 months…'; Gate 2 · Reasonable 'Extend observation past 12 months…'
questions.rationale: EASL and ACG indicate resection at 6 months. At that point only 8.5-15.3% of adenomas over 5 cm have fallen below 5 cm, against 23.7-27.1% at 52 weeks and 58.5% eventually at a median 104 weeks, with no complication during the whole of that follow-up and time to regression strongly size-dependent (median 63 weeks under 7 cm, 208 weeks over 10 cm). The six-month trigger therefore captures roughly one in six to one in ten of the lesions that will eventually regress below 5 cm. The cohort's authors proposed 12 months for typical non-beta-catenin adenomas in women; 79% of responding European experts already decline the rule; and the only GRADE-appraised guideline grades the 6-month decision point very low quality, conditional. Decide the number, and decide whether it differs by baseline diameter.
questions.audit: Audit: time to fall below 5 cm or to intervention, for every adenoma over 5 cm under surveillance.

questions.title: Does the programme resect every male adenoma irrespective of size, and is expert liver pathology review with sequencing mandatory in every male case?
questions.question: Does the programme resect every male adenoma irrespective of size, and is expert liver pathology review with sequencing mandatory in every male case?

positions.says: Resection or curative treatment for every adenoma in a man, irrespective of size, because of a higher incidence of malignant transformation (II-3, grade 2).
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard 'Resect, irrespective of size…'

positions.says: Also recommends resection in men, as does ACG 2024, but grades it very low quality of evidence (D), conditional.
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard 'Resect, irrespective of size…'; Gate 3 · Reasonable option 'Resection'

positions.says: Tertiary series of 218 patients: transformation in 47% of men against 4% of women; transformed lesions had a median 10 cm diameter. The roadmap reads 47% as a near-maximum referral figure, not a population risk.
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard 'Resect, irrespective of size…' (caveat and note)

positions.says: Expert revision plus sequencing changed the diagnosis in 33 of 66 men (50%) and found 4 beta-catenin mutations missed by immunohistochemistry and re-review; the roadmap notes no comparator and mismatched mortality denominators.
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard 'Send every male adenoma for expert liver pathology review…'

positions.says: 78% of men resected for a presumed adenoma had a changed final diagnosis, and male sex independently predicted a change (aOR 3.7).
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard 'Send every male adenoma for expert liver pathology review…'

questions.divergence: The guidelines concur on resecting all men, but the transformation figures come from selected surgical series in which sex and size cannot be separated, and the male diagnosis is itself unreliable, so the rule may rest on risk or on diagnostic doubt.
questions.proposal: Resect every male adenoma irrespective of size (grade C), treating it as possibly already malignant, and send every male case, including outside diagnoses, for expert liver pathology review with sequencing before accepting the diagnosis (grade D). Observing a sequenced, confidently low-risk lesion in a prohibitive operative candidate is a documented exception requiring a board decision.
questions.proposal_locator: Gate 3 · Standard 'Resect, irrespective of size…' and 'Send every male adenoma for expert liver pathology review…'; Gate 3 · Reasonable option 'Observation with a sequenced, confidently low-risk subtype'; What we are not sure about #12-13
questions.rationale: EASL, ACG and the Italian guideline all say resect, the last of them at very low quality of evidence, conditional. The male evidence is a 47% versus 4% transformation prevalence in one tertiary surgical series whose transformed lesions had a median diameter of 10 cm, an approximately ten-fold male excess in a second, and male sex as an independent predictor at an odds ratio of 18.9 (8.5-44.2). Against that, the diagnostic label is unreliable in exactly this group: 50% of presumed male adenomas are reclassified on expert review with 4 beta-catenin mutations found only by sequencing, and 78% of male resections in a national audit had their diagnosis changed. The full-text read also withdrew the 23.8% occult-carcinoma figure this page previously used — the supported figure is 4 transformations in 27 male adenomas — and found no cohort supporting observation of any male adenoma. So the question is whether the rule is retained because men are at higher risk or because the diagnosis cannot be trusted in men; the answer changes what the pathology requirement is for.
questions.audit: Registry: sex, size, subtype, sequencing result, decision, specimen finding.

questions.title: Is elective transarterial embolisation accepted as a first-line alternative to resection in a good surgical candidate who prefers it?
questions.question: Is elective transarterial embolisation accepted as a first-line alternative to resection in a good surgical candidate who prefers it?

positions.says: Embolisation is an alternative to resection for larger lesions but the treatment of choice only in poor surgical candidates; residual viable lesion afterwards is an indication for resection.
positions.locator: Gate 4 · Standard option group, 'Transarterial embolisation'; Gate 7 · Reasonable 'Transarterial embolisation of the dominant lesions…' (caveat)

positions.says: Elective embolisation avoided surgery in 41 of 49 patients (84%); the roadmap notes small mixed series, a process endpoint, a 31-month pooled follow-up and no separate elective complication rate.
positions.locator: Gate 4 · Standard option group, 'Transarterial embolisation'; What we are not sure about #16

positions.says: In 59 patients median diameter fell from 76 to 48 mm, but grade D complications occurred in 10%, one patient died three months later, 34% still needed surgery and symptoms did not improve (P=0.134).
positions.locator: Gate 4 · Standard option group, 'Transarterial embolisation' (caveat); What we are not sure about #16

questions.divergence: EASL confines embolisation to poor surgical candidates; later series report frequent surgery avoidance and shrinkage, but with a reported death, a third still operated, no symptom benefit and no histology.
questions.proposal: Embolisation stays on the page (grade C) for a large, central or bilobar lesion where resection would be major, or a patient who wants to avoid an operation and accepts imaging follow-up, with harms disclosed in consent; in multiple adenomas its use is recorded as a departure from EASL. The roadmap does not itself endorse or decline first-line elective use.
questions.proposal_locator: Gate 4 · Standard option group, 'Transarterial embolisation'; Gate 7 · Reasonable 'Transarterial embolisation of the dominant lesions…'; What we are not sure about #16
questions.rationale: EASL reserves embolisation for poor surgical candidates. The data since show 84% surgery avoidance after elective embolisation, on 49 patients from multiple small series, and a fall in median diameter from 76 to 48 mm. Against that: 10% grade D complications, one reported death three months after the procedure, 34% of patients still requiring surgery, no symptom improvement at 3 months (P=0.134), viable tissue and no histology left behind in a disease where 20-40% of presumed adenomas prove to be something else, and a pooled follow-up of 31 months too short to detect transformation. That is a shared decision the programme should endorse or decline explicitly, with the harms disclosed, rather than leave to individual preference.
questions.audit: Registry: modality, diameter change, complication grade, subsequent intervention.

questions.title: What is the acute haemorrhage pathway, and who owns it out of hours?
questions.question: What is the acute haemorrhage pathway, and who owns it out of hours?

positions.says: Embolise the haemodynamically unstable bleeding adenoma (evidence level III, grade 2); resuscitate and transfer to a centre that can embolise; admit for observation and contrast CT when haemorrhage is clinically evident.
positions.locator: Gate 5 · Standard 'Resuscitate with blood products…' and 'Admit and observe the stable patient…'

positions.says: Before 24 weeks, surgery may be preferred to embolisation for smaller peripheral resections because of fetal radiation and contrast exposure; in an exsanguinating patient the fastest route wins, per the roadmap.
positions.locator: Gate 5 · Avoid 'Do not embolise a pregnant patient before 24 weeks…'

positions.says: Review proposing the acute algorithm: practice has shifted from resection to initial conservative management with selective embolisation. The roadmap cites it from abstract only and calls this gate weakly sourced.
positions.locator: Gate 5 · Standard 'Resuscitate with blood products…' (caveat); Provenance

positions.says: Surgery was avoided in 68 of 151 embolised patients (45%), a figure mixing elective and acute indications; the roadmap says who needs a second procedure is identified by re-imaging.
positions.locator: Gate 5 · Standard 'Re-image once stable…'

questions.divergence: Sources agree on embolisation first in the unstable patient, but only at evidence level III with no comparative series, and none defines the re-imaging interval, the transfer route or out-of-hours ownership.
questions.proposal: Resuscitate, obtain contrast CT and transfer to an embolisation-capable centre; admit and observe contained bleeding without acute surgery; re-image once stable (MRI at 6-12 weeks, a convention) and resect residual viable lesion. Limited resection is reasonable for a small peripheral exophytic lesion where no embolisation exists. A same-day board route exists; no out-of-hours owner is named.

questions.rationale: Not an evidence question. EASL's recommendation to embolise the unstable patient is evidence level III, and the practical failure mode is a young woman arriving at a hospital that cannot embolise, with no named transfer route. The interval to the post-embolisation re-imaging that decides whether she needs a resection is also undefined by any study.
questions.audit: Audit: haemorrhage events with size, position, management route, time to definitive control, and whether residual viable lesion was resected.

questions.rationale: This item cannot be decided yet, and that is now the honest answer. The positional and vascular effect sizes this page previously quoted in support could not be confirmed in the full-text read and have been withdrawn; what the supporting paper does establish is a fitted cut-point at 35 mm with bleeding in 5.4% below against 53% above, in a retrospective cohort whose own protocol used 5 cm to decide which lesions were resected, with grades I to III pooled, no beta-catenin adenoma identified in 195 lesions and 48% unclassifiable. Adopting a composite trigger would mean operating on some lesions below 5 cm, which no guideline endorses. Before deciding, someone should read that paper's positional analysis directly and report the numbers.

questions.question: Does the transplant protocol's S45 and exon 7/8 restriction stand as written?

positions.locator: Gate 10 · Standard 'Name the qualifying route in the narrative…'

positions.locator: Gate 10 · Standard 'Name the qualifying route in the narrative…' (caveat); Reference library

positions.locator: Gate 10 · Standard 'Name the qualifying route in the narrative…' (caveat); What we are not sure about #15

questions.rationale: The protocol places S45 exon 3 with the exon 7/8 alterations as not qualifying the molecular route alone. The genotype-phenotype data make S45 a special case rather than a low-risk one — a weak activator in benign tumours, found at similar frequency in mutated adenomas and carcinomas, and duplicated to high activity in most carcinomas. The restriction is defensible as organ stewardship but not as a statement about risk, and the NLRB narrative should say which of the two it is.

questions.rationale: Hepatocellular adenoma is not a standardised exception. The whole indication rests on 142 US transplants over 33 years with 18.3% mortality over a median 62.9 months and 9.0% waitlist mortality in patients of median age 34.5 and median MELD 8 — so almost all of that mortality is treatment-attributable — plus 49 European adenomatosis transplants with three operative deaths, five retransplantations, three fatal recurrences and true transformation in only 17 of 49 explants. The US registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas; the European one miscoded a quarter of its cases; neither has a comparison group managed without transplantation; and 61.3% of US recipients received exception points while about a tenth met the stated criteria. Graft stewardship for a benign disease is an institutional judgement, and it should be made with those numbers in front of the committee.
questions.audit: Registry required if opened: route named, lesion dataset, review-board decision, waitlist events, donor source, explant concordance, graft and patient survival.

Any required missing, pending or adverse determination is a HOLD. An exception application is not approval, a donor is not recipient benefit, and clinical approval is not study activation.
Recheck the current policy/guidance version before each request; record actual decision and priority rather than predicted entitlement.
shared.tests: Signed suitability record; exact allocation route and policy version; exception outcome; donor-team status; study and institutional activation record.
shared.allocation: Policy 9.4 permits discretionary requests where appropriate; absence of favorable diagnosis-specific guidance is not absence of a review mechanism, and a request does not promise approval.
shared.rationale: The separation is a governance requirement, not an empirical survival cutoff. A clinically appropriate patient can lack exception eligibility, and an approved exception does not prove clinical benefit. LDLT requires an independent donor determination; a registry entry is not permission to perform experimental transplantation.
shared.counter: Not every case needs six separate affirmative approvals: several routes are alternatives or not applicable. An indiscriminate six-approval rule could obstruct appropriate standard care.
shared.certainty: High confidence in the separation of applicable authorities; no trial establishes that six boxes improve survival. Local workflow must map to current institutional obligations.
threshold_basis: Six domains: local checklist architecture, not six mandatory national approvals.
100% applicable completion: governance safeguard, not an outcome-derived percentage.
Hold pending required authorization: operational implementation of separate clinical, donor and research responsibilities.

shared.proposal: Require two independent recipient-benefit reviews and an explicit organ-use case; do not adopt a universal five-year survival cutoff.
rules: Proposed requirements: two reviewers not both responsible for recruitment must document expected incremental benefit over the actual contemporary alternative, with unresolved disagreement referred to the full committee.

For DDLT, show local expected access/dropout and sensitivity scenarios at 6, 12 and 18 months, total graft use including retransplantation, and plausible alternative recipients. These are planning scenarios, not imposed waiting periods.

For LDLT, separately show healthy-donor risk and potential downstream deceased-donor graft use. Do not call DCD, extended-criteria grafts or machine perfusion “zero opportunity cost.” No priority changes follow from an AI-selected survival threshold.
shared.tests: Same-eligibility/time-zero comparator; expected access; dropout; donor/graft type; uncertainty intervals; graft loss/retransplant estimate; written independent reviews.
shared.allocation: Only the applicable allocation process determines priority. Favorable post-LT prognosis, evidence grade and urgency are not interchangeable measures.
shared.rationale: Use pathway-level benefit from an agreed entry date, not recipient-only survival. Compare with contemporary tumor-specific care and actual local access. LDLT avoids one direct deceased-donor allocation but creates healthy-donor risk and may generate rescue graft use. Graft quality/perfusion changes do not make opportunity cost zero.
shared.counter: An ambitious prognosis threshold can exclude patients with substantial incremental benefit, while an indolent tumor can have excellent post-LT survival and little incremental benefit. Local wait times and unequal access can reverse a study’s apparent advantage.
shared.certainty: Benefit evidence differs by disease: randomized selected CRLM/HCC pathways cannot be generalized to all expanded indications. Ethical principles are authoritative frameworks, not empirically optimized allocation weights.
threshold_basis: Two reviewers: local independence safeguard, not validated optimum.
6/12/18 months: sensitivity scenarios for access/dropout, not mandatory waits.
HCC ≥60% five-year ITT OS: one expert trial-design benchmark; not a cross-cancer allocation policy.
All grafts: count initial and rescue/retransplant grafts; donor morbidity remains a separate outcome.

studies.population: Multicenter randomized phase 2b/3 trial: 74 entered downstaging; 29 dropped out before randomization; 45 responders were randomized, 23 to LT and 22 to nontransplant treatment. Child-Pugh A–B7, ECOG 0–1, predicted five-year post-LT survival ≥50%, and ≥3 months sustained response. AFP rules depended on baseline value and response, not an unconditional AFP <400 entry rule.
studies.results: From randomization, five-year overall survival was 77.5% with LT versus 31.2% without LT; tumor-event-free survival 76.8% versus 18.3%; median follow-up 71 months.
studies.limits: Strongest causal evidence for LT among selected responders, not for all 74 entrants or unlimited initial burden. Small, prematurely stopped trial. Appendix allowed uncertain bland-versus-neoplastic segmental/type-I portal thrombosis under additional response conditions; the actual PVTT denominator/outcomes are not reported. It must not be relabeled a proven-PVTT trial.
studies.locator: Complete accepted manuscript and protocol appendix; final published abstract for survival estimates. Avoid mixing accepted-manuscript and final-publication hazard ratios.

studies.population: Multicentre open-label randomized trial, 20 European centres, 157 screened and 94 randomized (47 LT-plus-chemotherapy, 47 chemotherapy); 63 screened excluded, including 13 with equivocal unresectability and 36 with progression. Age 18–65; ECOG 0–1; R0 colorectal primary; BRAF nonmutated; no prior or current extrahepatic disease/local recurrence; chemotherapy response or stable disease for at least 3 months, at most three lines. CEA <80 ng/mL OR at least 50% reduction from peak was permitted. Independent committee of at least two surgeons, two oncologists and one radiologist reviewed original and current lesion maps. These are trial criteria, not identical to current NLRB guidance.
studies.results: Primary time origin was randomization. Median follow-up 59.3 months. Five-year ITT OS was 56.6% versus 12.6% (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.65); per-protocol OS 73.3% versus 9.3%. Of 47 assigned LT, 38 received LT and 36 were per-protocol; nine had progression-related exclusion/dropout. The control arm included seven subsequent resections and two LT crossovers. Safety population comprised 40 grafted patients. Among 36 per-protocol LT recipients, 26 recurred; 19/26 received chemotherapy and 12/26 local curative-intent treatment. Median per-protocol PFS was 17.4 versus 6.4 months, and secondary PFS after salvage was 35.4 months in the LT arm. Three of 36 per-protocol recipients required retransplantation (primary nonfunction, donor gallbladder cancer, caval obstruction/large-for-size); one postoperative death was reported. Serious adverse events occurred in 32/40 safety LT recipients. Median wait to LT was 50.5 days, which limits transfer to longer-wait systems.
studies.limits: Strong evidence for the selected trial population, not for BRAF-mutant, ECOG 2, active extrahepatic, truly NED, resectable or broadly expanded disease. PP survival conditions on reaching treatment and must not replace ITT. The Results recurrence denominator is 26/36; Figure 3 caption says 28 recurrences, consistent with a broader all-grafted report, so do not mix these denominators. QoL collection had only 55/74 per-protocol baseline questionnaires and is descriptive, not proof of a large QoL gain. Priority allocation and rapid access were part of the treatment strategy.
studies.locator: Lancet 2024;404:1107–1118. PDF pp.2–4 eligibility/committee; pp.5–6 trial flow/Table 1; pp.8–9 recurrence, safety, retransplantation, Figure 3; p.10 QoL/limitations.

studies.population: UK national liver-offering policy evaluation: separate simulation dataset of 1,287 registrations/629 donors plus early real-world NLOS implementation, 2018–2020. Transplant-benefit scoring governed national deceased-donor offers; not a high-risk-HCC validation sample.
studies.results: Simulation compared observed 2013 deaths/removals 93 (7%) and 4,581 patient-years with modeled TBS outcomes 48 (4%) and 5,262 patient-years. studies.limits: Simulated gains are not observed outcomes. Before/after implementation is nonrandomized and can reflect secular changes. Nonetheless it is meaningful evidence that a governed benefit-based system can be deployed, unlike a claim that all such models are unusable.

rules: Proposed readiness requirements: independent donor evaluation/advocacy, documented freedom to withdraw, recipient-benefit uncertainty consent, and funded medical, psychological, recovery and financial follow-up before investigational LDLT.

Proposed local follow-up: baseline, six weeks, six months, one year, two years, then annually through five years. Meet current OPTN reporting duties separately; this five-year support plan is not claimed to be a national reporting requirement.

One donor death, life-threatening complication, permanent major disability or liver failure requiring transplantation triggers an immediate pause of the relevant investigational LDLT activity and independent review. shared.tests: Graft/resection-specific and center-specific risk; donor recovery/employment baseline; independent consent and advocate records; funded follow-up/support; sentinel-event response owner.
shared.allocation: LDLT clearance is separate from recipient selection; the potential need for retransplantation must be included in organ-use discussions.
shared.rationale: Donor mortality is low but not zero; complication, recovery and financial burdens are more frequent. Registry missingness and selected healthy donors limit reassurance. shared.counter: Older A2ALL complication rates and modern SRTR mortality are different outcomes from overlapping eras/cohorts; do not pool them. Five-year support is a reasonable local response to late morbidity, not a proven optimal schedule. Social vulnerability should trigger assistance, not categorical exclusion.
shared.certainty: Moderate certainty for the existence of material donor burden; lower certainty for individual risk and long-term recovery because of incomplete follow-up. No oncology-specific randomized donor-safety comparison.
threshold_basis: Baseline/6 weeks/6 months/1/2 years then annually to five: proposed support schedule; current mandatory reporting remains separately checked.
One sentinel event: conservative review/pause trigger, not a statistically estimated harm boundary.
No relaxed donor criteria: protection against shifting uncertain recipient benefit onto a healthy person.

shared.proposal: Use a small staged pilot with all-screened accounting and explicit safety pauses; no automatic expansion on favorable recipient survival.
rules: Proposed initial cap: ten transplants per separately approved biological stratum. Review after the first five have 90-day follow-up; no expansion decision until all first ten have at least 12-month follow-up. Reconcile vital status, graft events and known serious harms for every participant; require ≥90% completeness for other prespecified key outcomes.

In an initial experimental cohort, one all-cause recipient death, graft loss or retransplantation within 90 days triggers a pause of further experimental enrollment/transplantation pending independent review. A later possibly treatment-related death/graft loss or a donor sentinel event also triggers review/pause. Rescue care is never withheld; reopening requires independent authorization.

These are proposed conservative review triggers, not statistically validated efficacy/futility boundaries. Before opening, biostatistics and the independent board must ratify or replace them with indication-specific rules, denominators, pause authority and reopening criteria.

Capture every screened candidate, including nonrecipients, conversion to resection, dropout, deaths and access barriers; report survival from entry and from LT, recurrence, graft use, donor recovery and quality of life. Ten survivors alone do not establish benefit or authorize expansion.
shared.tests: Locked eligibility strata; prospective entry/time-zero dataset; modern comparator; adverse-event definitions; follow-up-completeness report; independently signed statistical and safety plan.
shared.allocation: Study monitoring never changes exception criteria or guarantees future access. Audit access by referral, geography, resources and donor availability without turning protected characteristics into exclusion rules.
shared.rationale: A small pilot can test feasibility, staging fidelity, data capture and acute safety, not prove durable survival benefit. Define time zero, all-screened enrollment, waitlist failures, post-LT survival/recurrence, competing death, all grafts, donor harms and patient-reported outcomes before opening. An independent board needs actual pause/reopening authority.
shared.counter: Zero observed events among ten fully followed independent patients still has a one-sided exact 95% binomial upper bound of 25.9% (1−0.05^(1/10)). Thus ten survivors cannot establish a <5% event risk. Ninety percent data completeness permits one missing patient; safety events and vital status require active ascertainment, not tolerance of unaccounted loss.
shared.certainty: Strong methodological rationale for predefinition and ITT accounting; no empirical validation of our exact cap/interim/completeness thresholds. Late recurrence demands multi-year follow-up.
threshold_basis: Ten per stratum and interim after five at 90 days: local feasibility cap and safety review cadence.
Twelve-month minimum: earliest expansion discussion, not proof of long-term cancer benefit.
≥90%: proposed non-vital key-measure completeness threshold; not permission to ignore deaths/graft events or unknown status.
One early death/graft loss/re-LT: review/pause trigger, not automatic futility or withholding rescue.
